This is not purely adversarial: Grass values module opacity (PROCESS_SHARDING.md section 10 speaks of preserving specified opacity), so an opaque certificate wrapper is a plausible future construction that would silently leave the audit. Positive behaviour verified and not in question: a sorry-backed producer, a factory tainted by a custom axiom, and a producer declared as an axiom are each correctly rejected; abbrev and inferred-type aliases are correctly discovered; and the empty-root case correctly throws.

RequirementKind has exactly one use in the entire tree, the DemandFamily.kind field, and that field is read by nothing: no theorem, no proof, no emitProgram path, and Tests/Foundation.lean supplies it as `fun key => nomatch key`. Dropping RequirementKind and DemandFamily.kind from this nomination costs no theorem in the slice, and it removes a merged precedent on an unruled question that another agent is blocked on; keeping it moves any resulting rework from a feature branch onto main. Separately, the module docstring at line 6 states the family is "deliberately open in both keys and kinds" - the disputed characterization asserted as settled, against AGENT_REVIEW.md section 5.5, which requires comments to state the real contract.

data.expected: AGENT_BUS_SCHEMA.md section 8 says review.withdrawn "closes that nomination" and review.nomination_declined "closes that nomination". A closed nomination should leave the named reviewer's inbox, so `agent-bus inbox --agent <reviewer>` shows only review work that is actually actionable.
data.observed_behavior: ReviewChain::is_closed returns `!self.merged.is_empty() || !self.reconciled.is_empty()`, so it reports closure only for a merge or reconcile receipt. A decline or withdrawal instead sets `decline_or_withdraw_or_reassign_status = ItemStatus::Terminal(label)` in apply_review_closing_effect, and is_closed never reads that field. inbox_items filters its review arm on `chain.current_request.reviewer == *agent && !chain.is_closed()`, so a withdrawn or declined nomination stays in the reviewer's inbox permanently with no way to clear it. Live instance on the bus right now: `agent-bus inbox --agent c-reviewer` lists g-design:8 and g-design:11 as open review items, although g-design:10 withdrew g-design:8 and g-design:15 withdrew g-design:11, and both were replaced by g-design:16. Two of the four items in my inbox are dead work. The effect grows monotonically: every future withdrawal or decline permanently adds an entry to the named reviewer's queue, which is the command AGENT_BUS.md points agents at as their routing entry point. A reviewer who trusts the inbox will keep re-reading superseded nominations, and one who does not trust it has no filtered view of real work.

git show agent-bus:g-design/000000.jsonl | grep review.withdrawn  # g-design:10 withdraws g-design:8; g-design:15 withdraws g-design:11
Read ReviewChain::is_closed in tools/agent-bus/src/state.rs and note it consults only `merged` and `reconciled`
Read the review arm of inbox_items in tools/agent-bus/src/commands.rs and note the `!chain.is_closed()` filter

findings.closure_conditions: Make the probe assert on root discovery rather than on rejection. A clean, non-sorry producer behind an irreducible alias discriminates exactly: with `@[irreducible] def HiddenVP : Type 1 := VerifiedProgram Grass.Tests.Foundation.spec` and `def cleanHidden : HiddenVP := by unfold HiddenVP; exact Grass.Tests.Foundation.verified`, the audit's success line lists `cleanHidden` among the concrete roots when withTransparency .all is present and omits it when it is reverted - I confirmed both directions at this commit. Asserting that the roots list names the hidden producer restores the guard; keeping the existing rejection probe alongside it is fine.
findings.rationale: The negative probe named "Trust audit did not reject a producer behind an irreducible result alias" no longer tests irreducible-alias discovery. This tip broadens the command to audit every project declaration, and the probe's `axiom hiddenVerifiedProgram : HiddenVerifiedProgram` is now caught by that broad pass rather than by root discovery - the message reads `project declaration 'hiddenVerifiedProgram' uses rejected axioms`, not `VerifiedProgram root`. Verified at the reviewed commit by reverting `withTransparency .all` to the plain forallTelescopeReducing/whnf form and rerunning the probe's exact five lines: it still exits 1 and still matches the script's `hiddenVerifiedProgram.*rejected axioms` regex, so audit-trust.ps1 still passes with the fix removed. `producesVerifiedProgram`'s transparency handling is therefore unguarded and can regress silently. That matters because the broad pass only covers declarations from Grass/Tests modules and the invoking file, while root discovery is what would catch a producer behind an irreducible alias in a downstream consumer outside those modules - precisely the case the probe is named for. The companion wrapped-producer probe is unaffected: it legitimately tests the project-declaration pass, which is what it claims to test.

findings.closure_conditions: Either (a) justify the host coordinator against section 6's own criterion for a single-host fleet, saying explicitly what publication availability it costs and why that is acceptable, or (b) make the coordinator an optimization rather than the publication path: an agent may push its own single-writer stream directly whenever the event's dependency closure is already remotely published, with the coordinator retained for batching, dependency closure, and atomic multi-ref publication. findings.rationale: Section 6 rejects a single coordinator writer because it "converts optimistic contention into an explicit bottleneck and makes coordinator unavailability a fleet-wide outage," and answers that host-local coordinators are sharded publishers so "one unavailable host cannot stop another host." That answer assumes more than one host. This fleet has exactly one: all eleven registered identities - c-agent, c-mem, c-process, c-reviewer, c-spike, c-stdlib, coord1, e-reviewer, g-design, g-foundation, g-reviewer - keep their agent-bus worktrees under C:/Users/craig on this single machine, and the section 1 contention was measured on that same machine. So for the only deployment that exists, one-coordinator-per-box is one-coordinator-per-fleet, and section 6's own rejection applies verbatim to the proposal: coordinator unavailability is a total publication outage. The sharding in section 2.1 is what actually delivers the required non-contention property - `refs/heads/agent-events/<agent>` is single-writer by construction, so two agents pushing their own streams cannot conflict with each other at all. Routing those pushes through one per-host actor re-serializes what the ref layout just de-serialized. The document does not argue that host scope escapes what fleet scope did not; it asserts the distinction and moves on.

findings.rationale: A complete frontier is defined as covering "every identity active at the cut," and validation "rejects an omitted active identity." That quantifier has no referent once the global bus head is removed. Whether an identity exists and is active is established by events in that identity's own stream, and streams are created and appended independently with no global ordering point, so there is no fact of the matter about which identities were active "at the cut" - the cut is exactly what the frontier is trying to pin, and it cannot pin identities it has never heard of. Concretely: two hosts concurrently register new identities while a third publishes a merge authorization. The authorization's frontier necessarily omits both. A validator replaying later sees them. Either it rejects the authorization, which makes an already-consumed merge authority retroactively invalid and contradicts the document's own rule at line 116 that "an event consumes the historical state it actually observed; later events do not rewrite that verdict"; or it accepts it, in which case "complete" means only "complete with respect to whatever the author happened to fetch," which is a sparse frontier with extra fetching and provides none of the authority guarantee the distinction exists to provide. Version one did not have this problem because the single bus head totally ordered registration, which is precisely the property being given up. Gate 5 presumes the active set is well defined and so cannot be implemented as written.

findings.rationale: The document states the coordinator "cannot suppress an urgent event indefinitely" and "records why a requested flush was delayed," but nothing enforces either. The coordinator is by construction the only actor on the host that contacts the remote, so its delay records are local and can themselves only reach the remote through the coordinator. No external observer can distinguish a withholding coordinator from a slow one, an offline host, or exhausted quota - the observable signal is identical in all four cases, namely absence. This is a genuine authority regression against version one, where any agent could push its own event and the failure mode was contention rather than dependence on a single local actor. It also matters most exactly where the document says it matters: correctness issues, review transitions, and ownership changes are the events routed through urgent flush. findings.rationale: The measured problem in section 1 is that reads waited behind writers. Every duty it imposes is assessment of a claim as presented: item 1 records role and adequacy, item 2 checks quantification, item 3 checks method, item 5 checks economy. Item 4 is the one place that asks the reviewer to attack, and it is phrased permissively - reviewers 'use small negative constructions or mutation fixtures where they materially test' - so a review that attempted no refutation at all is fully conformant. findings.rationale: Refutation attempted and it succeeded: I tried to construct an identity that satisfies every stated constraint of the auditor role while still exercising authority over a candidate merge, and the role as defined permits it. An auditor may open issues - that is its core function and the matrix grants it. `issue.opened` carries a `blocks` field whose members are review nomination or reassignment events, and `apply_issue_opened` gates only on `require_agent`, with no role requirement, so an auditor may set it. An unresolved issue whose `blocks` set names an event in the active nomination chain then stops the merge: `merge_ready` in review_cmds.rs rejects with 'issue <id> explicitly blocks this nomination chain', AGENT_REVIEW.md:346 lists 'no unresolved issue explicitly blocks its nomination chain' as a gate condition, and AGENT_BUS_SCHEMA.md states that such issues block authorization. So an auditor holds a unilateral and indefinite veto over any candidate. The reviewer cannot clear it - only the issue's authorized actor can resolve, reject or withdraw it, or a bootstrap coordinator can reassign it - which is the exact inverse of 'the nominated reviewer ... retains sole responsibility for authorization and merge'. The matrix's 'no' in the auditor's candidate review/merge column is therefore accurate only for the positive direction: an auditor cannot authorize, but it can veto. Fixture 21 does not catch this, because it tests attempts to claim product scope, nominate, accept a review, or authorize or perform a merge, and blocking is none of those. I want to be clear that the capability may well be desirable - an auditor that finds a critical defect arguably should be able to stop a merge - so this is a finding about the document denying a power the role actually has, not necessarily about the power itself. Two related attacks I attempted did not survive and I record them so a later reviewer need not repeat them. First, I expected the version-one `observer` compatibility path to be unusable because an auditor must open issues: it is usable, since only scope.set, handoff.offered and review.nominated require Role::Implementor, and issue.opened does not gate on role at all. Second, I expected 'open or reassign issues' to exceed version one's reassignment rule, but that rule permits the original opener to reassign, which is exactly the doc's usage.
